title: 2.7.1 Individual PA Part 1: Concepts and Traces
description: Eight questions: three on the ideas of Chapter 2, five where you read a short program and say what it prints. One submission, nothing marked on screen.

questions.question: Chapter 2 added the first conditional to your toolkit. Which statement about `if (x == true)` is correct?
options: It is the preferred way to test a boolean
It is redundant if x is already a boolean
It is required because `if (x)` doesn't work
It is the only way to check for truthiness
questions.explanation: If a value is already a boolean, writing `if (x == true)` is redundant. The conditional directly uses the truthiness of x. Use `if (x)` instead.

questions.question: You are writing a program that makes a decision based on a comparison. Which paradigm are you using?
questions.explanation: A straight-line script with conditionals and loops that runs top to bottom is procedural/structured programming. Object-oriented needs objects/classes; functional avoids mutable state; declarative describes what, not how.

questions.question: You are drawing a flowchart for a program with a loop that has a decision inside it. Which shapes must appear?
questions.explanation: The loop requires a hexagon (§2.2), the decision needs a diamond, steps need rectangles, Start/End need ovals, and I/O uses parallelograms. That's five shapes total.

questions.explanation: Loose equality `==` converts both sides to numbers. `0 == false` converts `false` to 0, so `0 == 0` is true. The program prints 'empty'.

questions.explanation: With text on one side, `+` joins rather than adds, so `"10" + 5` builds the text `105`. The `-` operator has no meaning for text, so JavaScript converts `"10"` to the number 10 and subtracts, giving 5.

questions.explanation: `Number("ten dollars")` produces `NaN`. Every arithmetic operation with `NaN` produces `NaN`, so it travels through the addition and subtraction unchanged.
